title: Quarto Portfolio & Learning Hub — Master Project Context
text:
Use this document as the handoff context whenever continuing this website with ChatGPT, Claude, or another coding assistant. Treat the website as an existing project that must be developed incrementally, not rebuilt from scratch.


This is Paing Hein Soe’s Quarto-based Portfolio & Learning Hub.
Local Windows project root:
D:\Portfolio_Drive\Quarto_website
Primary working environment: - Quarto website project - Visual Studio Code - Windows PowerShell - HTML output generated by Quarto - Custom CSS in styles.css - Small custom JavaScript for article counts - GitHub / GitHub Pages is the intended publishing path, but the current Git/repository/publishing state must be checked rather than assumed.



The site has two related purposes.


The portfolio should present professional background, experience, research, selected projects, publications, and technical skills with enough depth to show the actual work behind a resume. It should not simply duplicate a CV. Project pages should emphasize the problem, role, data/methods, analysis, results, visuals, and what was learned or contributed.



The learning hub is a place to publish useful articles based on topics being learned, used, tested, or applied. The goal is not to produce generic blog content. Articles should help a reader understand a topic or reproduce a workflow.
The main topic areas are: 1. Energy & Climate 2. AI & Agents 3. Data Analytics 4. Programming & Technology
The overall site should make sense to both professional visitors (employers, collaborators, researchers) and readers who come for practical learning material.




These rules are important and should be preserved in every new article or revision.

Do not write in a generic AI-generated article style.
Prefer a natural, direct, thoughtful, technically accurate voice.
Avoid inflated introductions, marketing language, repetitive encouragement, filler, and predictable phrases such as “in today’s rapidly evolving world.”
Do not make the author sound like an expert on something merely because an AI can explain it. Where appropriate, write from the perspective of someone learning, testing, applying, or documenting the workflow.
Explain not only what to do, but why the step matters, what the reader should expect to see, and what can go wrong.
Use exact commands, filenames, paths, screenshots, tables, diagrams, code snippets, or checkpoints when they genuinely make the workflow easier to understand.
Keep technical explanations accessible without becoming shallow.
Use practical examples and real project context whenever possible.
Be transparent about assumptions, limitations, uncertainty, and sourced facts.
For current factual claims, software behavior, or external technical guidance, verify against authoritative sources when needed.
Visuals should add information or reduce confusion, not act as decorative filler.

A good article often includes: - a clear explanation of the topic; - an organized workflow or sequence; - practical examples or applications; - screenshots/figures where useful; - checkpoints showing what should happen; - common questions, pitfalls, or troubleshooting notes; - a short, natural conclusion or next step.
Do not force every article into an identical template. The structure should serve the topic.



Current main navigation: - Home - My Portfolio - Articles - Topics - Energy & Climate - AI & Agents - Data Analytics - Programming & Technology - About
LinkedIn and GitHub icons are in the right side of the navbar. Search is enabled.

The current source uses a restrained, professional visual system rather than a flashy template.
Key colors from styles.css: - page background: #f7f4ef - surface: #ffffff - soft surface: #eee9e3 - charcoal: #252321 - secondary charcoal: #373330 - primary text: #252321 - secondary text: #68615b - warm rust/chili accent: #a64232 - dark rust: #7f3025 - soft rust: #e4c2ba - border: #ddd5cc - main content width: about 1180px
The navbar and footer use charcoal. The rest of the site uses warm off-white/cream backgrounds, white cards, restrained borders/shadows, and rust accents.
The homepage currently uses a text-focused welcome panel. Earlier versions explored a dark hero, split image hero, gradient hero, and slider concepts, but those are not the current implementation. Do not reintroduce them unless specifically requested.
The current homepage flow is approximately: 1. Portfolio & Learning Hub welcome 2. Latest/recent articles (automatic Quarto listing, max 3) 3. Four topic-area cards 4. “Clear, Organized, and Easy to Follow” learning-hub explanation 5. Portfolio teaser / link
Design priorities: - readability first; - clear hierarchy; - generous whitespace; - professional rather than trendy; - consistent cards and spacing; - useful visual support; - responsive behavior on smaller screens.



_quarto.yml defines a website with the navigation above, search, LinkedIn/GitHub links, a dark footer, the Cosmo/theme setup, styles.css, smooth scrolling, external links opening in a new window, and article-counts.html included after the page body.
Do not change global configuration casually. Check how a change affects all pages before modifying _quarto.yml or global CSS.



articles.qmd lists articles/**/*.qmd, newest first, in a 3-column grid. It currently uses a page size of 9 and a filter UI.
Each topic page lists the .qmd files inside its corresponding article folder.
The homepage also lists recent articles automatically and shows at most three.
article-counts.js scans rendered article cards and fills the total/category counts shown on articles.qmd. This was added during iterative development. If the article collection grows beyond the listing page size or pagination behavior changes, re-check whether these counts still represent the full collection rather than only rendered cards.



The first real article is:
articles/programming-technology/getting-started-with-quarto.qmd
Title: Getting Started with Quarto
It is a beginner-oriented Windows guide that explains: - what Quarto, VS Code, and PowerShell each do; - installing Quarto and VS Code; - creating the workspace; - moving to the project directory with PowerShell; - creating a Quarto website; - previewing it locally; - understanding localhost; - editing index.qmd and seeing Quarto rebuild; - screenshots and checkpoints throughout.
The article intentionally explains the reasoning behind the steps instead of giving commands without context.
Its image assets are under:
images/quarto/
The article refers to them from its nested folder using paths such as:
../../images/quarto/download-vscode.png
When editing this article, preserve its practical teaching purpose but refine wording that feels repetitive or overly template-like. Repeated phrases such as “At this stage,” “Great,” “Congratulations,” or formulaic callouts should be used sparingly so the writing remains human and natural.



These three current articles are placeholders/test content used to make the listing/category system work: - articles/ai-agents/sample-ai-agents.qmd - articles/data-analytics/sample-data-analytics.qmd - articles/energy-climate/sample-energy-climate.qmd
They should not be treated as finished professional publications. Before public launch, replace them with genuine articles, mark them draft, or otherwise keep placeholder content from weakening the site’s credibility.
Earlier planning also anticipated future learning content related to Git/GitHub, Claude Code, Power BI, Python, software workflows, and similar practical topics. Add such content only as it is genuinely useful and relevant; do not create filler simply to populate categories.



Known items to address:

portfolio.qmd is still a placeholder and needs the actual professional portfolio architecture/content.
about.qmd is almost empty and needs a concise purpose/author/site explanation.
programming-technology.qmd currently has a line of body text before the opening YAML ---. The YAML front matter should be at the very top of the file; fix this before relying on a fresh render.
The Quarto tutorial currently describes the configuration file as quarto.yml; the actual Quarto website uses _quarto.yml. Correct the article.
_site/research.html exists although there is no current research.qmd source file. Treat this as stale generated output from an earlier iteration; _site should not be treated as source-of-truth.
.quarto/ and _site/ are generated/cache/output folders. Do not manually edit them.
Git/GitHub/GitHub Pages status is not established by the supplied project copy. Check it on the local machine rather than assuming it is configured.
The article-count JavaScript should be re-tested once there are more than 9 articles or if listing pagination/filter behavior changes.
The CSS contains some remnants from earlier iterations. Do not aggressively clean them until usage is checked, but later remove genuinely unused styles to reduce maintenance complexity.
The current project does not yet contain the complete portfolio assets/content anticipated in early planning (for example final resume/profile/project assets). Add them deliberately rather than dumping files into the repository.




When helping with this project:

Inspect the current file before proposing edits. Do not overwrite working architecture based on a generic Quarto template.
Treat index.qmd, _quarto.yml, styles.css, topic pages, and article files as established source files.
Never edit _site/ or .quarto/ as the solution; they are generated output/cache.
Make one logical change at a time where possible and explain what file is changing and why.
Preserve existing navigation, visual system, article directory structure, and relative image paths unless there is a specific reason to change them.
Give exact Windows/PowerShell commands when a local command is needed.
Avoid asking for files already present in the supplied project. Ask only for genuinely missing information.
If proposing substantial CSS or _quarto.yml changes, consider homepage, articles page, topic pages, article pages, and mobile behavior together.
Do not invent professional project results, publications, dates, affiliations, metrics, or skills. Ask for source material if needed.
For portfolio content, distinguish clearly between what belongs on a resume and what deserves deeper portfolio evidence.
For article content, prioritize accuracy and teaching value over SEO-style filler.
Where the current code is imperfect, fix it incrementally rather than starting over.
When debugging, first identify whether the issue is Quarto/YAML, file paths, listing behavior, CSS layout, JS, or generated-cache state.
Prefer quarto preview for local development and verify changes in the browser.




From Windows PowerShell:
cd D:\Portfolio_Drive\Quarto_website
quarto check
quarto preview
For Git status, if Git is installed:
git status
git branch --show-current
git remote -v
Do not assume the project is already a Git repository. Report the actual output first.



At the beginning of a new conversation, provide this context document and, when the code has changed substantially, the latest ZIP of Quarto_website.
Then use a short instruction such as:

Read the attached Quarto Portfolio & Learning Hub project context first. Treat it as an existing project and preserve the established purpose, architecture, visual system, and editorial principles. Inspect the current source files before recommending code. Do not rebuild it from a generic template. My task for this session is: [INSERT CURRENT TASK]. Ask me only for information or files that are genuinely missing.

The project context should be updated whenever major architecture, navigation, design, editorial rules, or publishing workflow changes. It does not need to be rewritten for every small article edit.

title: Getting Started with Quarto
text:
Have you been thinking about creating your own website to showcase your work, share projects, publish articles, or document what you are learning?
That is exactly what we are going to begin building together.
Getting started with Quarto is not difficult. However, the first setup can feel a little confusing because several tools are involved. We may naturally wonder:

What does Quarto actually do?
Why do we need Visual Studio Code?
What are we using PowerShell for?
What does quarto preview mean?
Has the website already been published when it opens in a browser?

These are completely normal questions.
In this guide, we will take the process one step at a time. We will not only copy commands—we will understand what each tool does, why we need it, and what we should expect to see after every step.
By the end, we will have a simple Quarto website running on our computer and a clear foundation for building a professional portfolio.
Although this guide demonstrates the setup on Windows, the overall workflow is almost identical on macOS. If you’re a Mac user, you can still follow along—the tools, concepts, and steps remain essentially the same, with only a few operating-system differences.






NoteQuarto is useful for more than portfolios



Although we are creating a portfolio website in this guide, the same setup can also be used to publish articles, present research, document projects, share ideas, or build a personal website.


Estimated time: 15 minutes

title: Getting Started with Quarto
Getting Started with Quarto
section: The Three Tools We Will Use 🧰
text:
The Three Tools We Will Use 🧰
Before starting, let us understand the role of each tool. Once these roles are clear, the entire process becomes much easier to follow.







Tool
What it does in this guide




Quarto
Builds the website by converting our .qmd writing files into webpages.


Visual Studio Code
Provides the workspace where we write, edit, organize, and manage the website files.


Windows PowerShell
Lets us send instructions to Quarto, such as creating the website project and starting a local preview.



Think of the workflow this way:
We write in VS Code
        ↓
PowerShell tells Quarto what to do
        ↓
Quarto builds the website
        ↓
The browser shows the result






TipDo we need to learn web programming first?



No. We will write mostly in Quarto Markdown, which is much simpler than building a website directly with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

title: Getting Started with Quarto
section: Step 1 — Install Quarto and Visual Studio Code
text:
Step 1 — Install Quarto and Visual Studio Code
We first need two applications:

Quarto, which will build the website.
Visual Studio Code, which we will use as our main writing and editing workspace.


Install Quarto
Open the official Quarto download page and download the installer for your operating system.
This guide uses Windows, so we will choose the Windows installer.



The official Quarto download page for Windows.








TipWhich Windows file should we choose?



For a normal Windows installation, the .msi installer is generally the simplest option. Open the downloaded file and follow the installation instructions.




Install Visual Studio Code
Next, open the official Visual Studio Code download page and choose the Windows version.



The official Visual Studio Code download page.


Visual Studio Code is not the program that builds the website. It is the workspace where we will open, write, and manage our website files.






ImportantThe roles are different



Quarto builds the website.
VS Code is where we work on it.
Keeping this distinction in mind will make the next steps much clearer.








NoteAfter installation



If PowerShell was already open while installing Quarto, close and reopen it. This allows Windows to recognize the newly installed quarto command.




Checkpoint ✅
At this stage, we should have:

Quarto installed;
Visual Studio Code installed;
access to Windows PowerShell.

Great—we now have the tools we need. Next, we will create a clean folder where our website can live.

title: Getting Started with Quarto
section: Step 2 — Create a Workspace for Your Portfolio
text:
Step 2 — Create a Workspace for Your Portfolio
What you’ll achieve: Create a dedicated location to keep your website organized from the beginning.
Before creating the website, it’s a good idea to prepare a workspace where all of your portfolio projects can live.
Although you could save the project anywhere, using a dedicated folder keeps everything organized and makes future projects much easier to manage.
For example, I created the following structure:



Recommended workspace for Quarto projects.


In this guide, my website is stored inside:
D:\Portfolio_Drive\Quarto_website
You can choose a different location if you prefer. The important idea is to keep your projects together rather than scattering them across different folders.






TipA small habit that saves time later



As you build more websites, notebooks, or research projects, having a dedicated workspace makes everything easier to find and maintain.



Checkpoint ✅
At this stage, we should have a folder ready for our Quarto website.

title: Getting Started with Quarto
section: Step 3 — Create Your First Quarto Website
text:
Step 3 — Create Your First Quarto Website
What you’ll achieve: Generate your first Quarto website and understand the files Quarto creates.
Now we’re ready to let Quarto create the website for us.

Open Windows PowerShell
Open Windows PowerShell and navigate to the folder you created.
For example:
cd D:\Portfolio_Drive\Quarto_website
The cd command stands for change directory. It simply tells PowerShell which folder we want to work in.



Navigate to the project folder using PowerShell.


Once you’re inside the correct folder, run:
quarto create project website .



Creating the Quarto website project.


Let’s briefly understand what this command means.



Part
Meaning




quarto
Runs the Quarto program.


create
Creates something new.


project
Creates a complete project instead of a single file.


website
Specifies that the project will be a website.


.
Creates the website in the current folder.









NoteWhat did Quarto just create?



Quarto automatically generated several files for us.

index.qmd — the homepage.
about.qmd — a second page for introducing yourself.
quarto.yml — the website configuration.
styles.css — optional custom styling.

Don’t worry about learning these files all at once. We’ll become familiar with them naturally as we continue building the website.




Checkpoint ✅
Congratulations! You now have a working Quarto website project.

title: Getting Started with Quarto
section: Step 4 — Open and Preview the Default Website
text:
Step 4 — Open and Preview the Default Website
What you’ll achieve: Open the project in Visual Studio Code, preview the default website, and understand how index.qmd becomes the homepage.
Open Visual Studio Code, then select:
File → Open Folder…
Choose your Quarto_website folder.
The project files should now appear in the Explorer panel on the left.



The Quarto website project opened in Visual Studio Code.



Preview the website
Open the terminal in Visual Studio Code, or return to PowerShell, and run:
quarto preview
Quarto builds the website and opens it in your browser.
Your browser should now display the default website created by Quarto.



The default Quarto website running locally in the browser.








NoteWhat does localhost mean?



The website is currently running only on your own computer.
It has not been published online yet.
Later, we’ll publish it online using GitHub Pages.




Compare the Source File with the Homepage
Now open index.qmd in Visual Studio Code.
You should see content similar to the following (the exact wording may vary slightly depending on your Quarto version):
---
title: "Quarto"
---

## Welcome

This is a Quarto website.
This is the source file that generates the homepage.
Compare the file above with the webpage shown in your browser.
Notice how the content in index.qmd appears on the webpage:



In index.qmd
On the homepage




title: "Quarto"
The page title


## Welcome
The main heading


This is a Quarto website.
The paragraph below the heading



This relationship is one of the most important ideas to understand when working with Quarto.
Every webpage starts as a .qmd file.
When you run:
quarto preview
Quarto converts that .qmd file into a webpage and displays it in your browser.
The workflow looks like this:
index.qmd
      ↓
quarto preview
      ↓
Quarto builds the webpage
      ↓
The browser displays the result






TipThink of it this way



Think of index.qmd as the source document.
Whenever you edit and save this file while quarto preview is running, Quarto automatically rebuilds the webpage and refreshes your browser.




Checkpoint ✅
At this stage, we should understand that:

index.qmd is the homepage source file;
quarto preview builds and displays the website;
the browser is showing a local preview, not a published website.

Next, we’ll edit index.qmd and watch the homepage change.

title: Getting Started with Quarto
text:
Step 5 — Personalize Your Homepage
What you’ll achieve: Replace the default homepage with your own introduction and watch Quarto update the website automatically.
Now let’s replace the default homepage with our own introduction.
Open index.qmd and replace its content with the following example:
---
title: "Welcome"
---

# Hello, I'm Paing Hein Soe 👋

I'm a Mechanical and Energy Engineer with interests in:

- Energy systems
- Artificial intelligence
- Data analytics
- Renewable energy
- Research

This website is where I share my projects, articles, and learning journey.

Thanks for visiting!
Save the file by pressing:
Ctrl + S
Since quarto preview is still running, Quarto automatically detects the change, rebuilds the website, and refreshes the browser.
Your homepage should now look similar to the following:



The personalized homepage after editing index.qmd.


Notice how your changes in index.qmd are immediately reflected in the browser.
The workflow is now:
Edit index.qmd
      ↓
Save the file
      ↓
Quarto automatically rebuilds the page
      ↓
The browser refreshes with the updated homepage






TipNo need to run quarto preview again



As long as quarto preview is still running, simply save your file whenever you make changes.
Quarto automatically rebuilds the website and refreshes the browser for you, making it easy to see your updates immediately.








NoteMake it your own



The example above uses my background for demonstration purposes.
When creating your own portfolio, replace the text with your own introduction, interests, projects, or professional background. The goal is to understand the editing process—not to copy the exact content.



Checkpoint ✅
🎉 You have now:

opened the website project in Visual Studio Code;
previewed the default Quarto website;
understood how index.qmd controls the homepage;
edited the homepage;
seen the website update automatically.

You have completed the basic Quarto workflow.
